item.title: Squeezing Out the Last 1% — torch.compile, Batch Inference, Pause Restoration, ARM64 - hayakoe Part 3
item.description:
Note: I’m based in Korea, so some context here is Korea-specific.

This is the third main installment of the hayakoe series. You can find the previous post at Halving Memory and Boosting Speed by 1.5× - hayakoe Part 2 .

In Part 2 , I made significant improvements to memory and speed via the main pillars — BERT Q8 quantization + Synthesizer ONNX conversion. But once I started actually running this model in production, I noticed a few things that felt unsatisfying, separate from the main pillars. They were the kind of work where I thought it would be nice to polish things into a more usable form.

item.title: Cutting Memory in Half and Speeding Up by 1.5x - hayakoe Part 2
item.description:
Note: I’m based in Korea, so some context here is Korea-specific.

This is the second main installment of the hayakoe series. You can read the previous post at hayakoe - After 2 Years, Trying Various TTS Models Again and Settling Back to VITS - Part 1 .

By the end of Part 1 , I had a trained model in hand, but as I noted in the introduction of the series, using that model as-is came with several inconveniences — the SPOF issue where openjtalk fetches dictionary data from an external server and dies along with it, the Python version upgrade blocked by that dependency, the fact that English synthesis didn’t work so I was routing through a translation layer, and the memory and speed burden I’ll cover in this post.

item.title: hayakoe - Building an Easy-to-Use, Fast TTS Library - Introduction
item.description:
Note: I’m based in Korea, so some context here is Korea-specific.

About two years ago, I came across a Japanese TTS library called Bert-VITS2, and I once wrote a post summarizing how to train it.

After that, I deployed the trained model on my home cluster server and had been using it casually. I forked the original code, then trimmed it down to keep only the path needed for voice synthesis.
